Nicholas  B^rault  (Beraldus)  of  Orleans  (c.  14-jo  —  p.  1545)  led  an  active  life  as 
a  teacher  and  as  an  editor  of  books.  He  was  a  contemporary  of  John  Pyrrhus 
d'AngIeberme  (Ep.  140  introd.),  and  became  Licentiate  in  Law,  probably  at 
Orleans  ;  where  after  a  visit  to  Italy  he  established  a  school,  which  in  1511  was 
of  some  size  (Aleander's  Jounial,  ed.  Omont,  pp.  19,  20).  His  first  publications 
were  editions  of  Bapt.  Mantuanus'  De  vita  beata,  Paris,  J.  Badius  (c.  Nov.  1505), 
and  Valla'3  Ekgantiae,  Paris,  W.  Hopyl  (c.  Feb.  1508).  "When  Aleander  began  to 
lecture  at  Orleans  in  1510-1,  Beraldus  was  one  of  his  audience  ;  but  c.  1512  he 
moved  to  Paris,  to  be  nearer  the  advantages  for  humanistic  study  now  offered  by 
the  capitJiL  He  lectured  in  the  colleges  and  continued  to  receive  pupils  into  his 
house  ;  and  his  activity  with  the  printers  was  great.  He  produced  editions  of 
Lucretius  1514,  Wm.  of  Auvergne'9  Operum  Summa  and  Pliny  N.  H.  i5i6,VaL 
Maximus  and  a  translation  of  Lucian's  Muscae  Encomium  151 7,  Athanasius  1519, 
Appian  and  a  new  edition  of  Craston's  Greek  Dictionary,  amplified  from  Hesy- 
chiusandSuidas,i52i,Theophylactusi534-.besidesundatededitionsofSuetonius, 
a  commentary  on  Aristotle's  Oeconomica,  and  Politian's  Rusticus.  About  the  end 
of  1515  he  married,  as  his  second  wife,  the  widow  of  .John  Barbier,  and  carried 
on  that  press  until  in  1518  he  found  the  work  too  much  for  him.  As  a  humanist 
he  enioyed  the  patronage  of  Stephen  Poncher  ;  whom  in  Aug.  1518  he  accom- 
panied  to  England  (cf.  Ep.  936.  25  n.),  with  introductions  from  Budaeus  to  Pace, 
More  and  Linacre(BE<.  18-20),  and  in  March  1519^0  Narbonne  (Ep.  924.  18  n.). 

For  some  years  he  continued  in  Paris,  taking  pupils  in  his  own  house  (cf. 
BE*  67)  •  among  these  c.  1525  being  Dolet  and  Wolmar,  the  future  master 
of  Calvin  His  sympathies  at  this  period  were  with  freedom  of  thought.  In 
editing  Athanasius  he  had  spoken  boldly  against  theologians,  and  thus  incurred 
the  hostility  of  the  Faculty  ;  which  in  1524  by  compellmg  him  to  rewrite  a  pre- 
face  he  had  composed  for  Chrysostom  suppressed  the  undertaking  altogether.  On 
Poncher's  death  (24  Feb.  1525)  he  was  taken  up  by  John  of  Orleans,  Abp. 
of  Toulouse  (+24  Sept.  1533).  and  in  1529  was  appomted  Eoyal  Historian 
in  succession  to  Paulus  Aemilius  'Ep.  136.  i  n.).

About  this  time  he  was  chosen  as  tutor  to  the  young  Colignys,  Gaapard, 
afterwards  Admiral  of  France,  and  his  elder  brother  Odet,  who  in  1533  at 
the  age  of  16  was  created  Cardinal,  and  in  1534  Abp.  of  Toulouse ;  and  with  thetn 
he  spent  some  years  at  Chatillon  sur  Loing  in  the  Orleanais.  In  1535  he  accom- 
panied  the  Cardinal  to  his  see  (EE*.  142 1,  where  he  made  the  acijuaintance  of 
John  de  Pins  (Ep.  928.  36  n.).  He  was  in  Paris  c.  March  1537  at  the  reception 
given  to  Dolet  on  his  release  from  prison  ;  and  was  still  in  Coligny's  service 
29  March  1538— tbe  last  certain  date  in  his  life. 

See  M.  Delaruelle  in  Rev.  des  Mbliolheques  xii  (1902),  421-45,  and  Mus^e  helge  xiii 
(1909,,  253-312;  also  BE,  and  R.  C.  Christie,  Etienne  Dolet.  Some  autograph 
letters  to  Beraldus  are  preserved  in  the  Public  Library  at  Beme  (see  H.  Hagen's 
catalogue  nos.  141,  450;  and  Herminjard  475,  483)  among  the  papers  of  Peter 
Daniel  ;  inherited  from  his  father  Francis  Daniel,  who  was  a  contemporary  of 
Beraldus  in  the  confidence  of  the  Coligny  family  (see  a  sketch  of  P.  Daniel  by 
H.  Hagen,  1873,  pp.  4-6;. 

Erasmus  first  met  Beraldus  in  1506,  when,  on  his  way  to  Italy,  he  was 
received  as  a  guest  in  his  house  at  Orleans  for  some  days.  Ten  years  later 
when  this  was  recalled  to  his  memory  (Ep.  494.  65-9),  he  responded  with  an 
eloquent  description  of  Beraldus'  natural  gifts  for  teaching  ( Ep.  535.  38-49). 
Their  relations  continued  friendly  throughout  their  lives.  In  1522  lie  dedicated 
to  Beraldus  the  authorized  edition  of  the  De  conscribendis Epistolis  (Ep.  71  introd.)  ; 
and  in  editing  Pliny  in  1525  he  speaks  highly  of  his  attainments  as  a  scholar 
(Lond.  xxviii.  14,  LB.  730).]

13.  Deberquino]  Louis  of  Berquin, 
near  Abbeville  (c.  1490  —  T7  April 
1529)  was  born  at  Patsy,  near  Paris, 
of  a  family  connected  with  tliat  of

Orleans,  where  he  was  intimate  with

came  into  contact  with  Badius  ;  who 
in  June  1512  dedicated  to  him  vol.  ii  of 
Politian's  Opera,  vol.  i  being  addressed 
to  Beraldus.  Badius  also  dedicated  to 
him  Aulus  Gellius  in  Sept.  151 7  ;  and 
Beraldus  his  translation  of  Lucian'd 
Muscae  Encmiium  and  an  edition  of 
FiIeIfo"s  Cotiuiuia,  Paris,  H.  Faber,  s.  a.

for  Erasmus  describes  him  as  dear  to 
Francis  i  and  as  Praefect  and  Eoyal 
Councilloi-  (Lond.  xxx.  44,  LB.  823). 
In  May  1523  the  Sorbonne  suddenly 
moved  the  Parliament  of  Paris  to  seize 
his  papers  ;  and  as  a  result  he  was  im- 
priaoned  till  Aug.,  when  the  King 
ordered  his  release.  His  offence  was 
that  he  had  begun  to  translate  into 
French  writings  by  Luther  and  Eras- 
mus ;  including,  of  the  latter,  the

Mairimonii  (Ep.  604.  10  n.;,  towhichhe

theless  were  printed  about  that  time 


by  Simon  Dubois  (Herminjard  259, 
n.  28).  In  Jan.  1526  he  was  arrested

Amiens  ;  propositions  from  his  works

career  'EE.  89),  and  c.  March  1529

I  Maxcli,  when  the  Apology  for  the  De  laude  matrimonii  was  completed.  But  he 
perhaps  went  shortly  afterwards  to  Mechlin  ;  for  the  word  reMerim  (1.  3)  suggests

did  not  stay  at  Mechlin  long  after  21  March  ;  for  by  28  March  he  had  finished 
tlie  Apology  against  Latomus  (Ep.  934.  3  n.),  which  was  a  work  of  two  or  three 
daya  CEpp.  948.  42,  952. 19,20),  and  was  presumably  written  at  Louvain.  A  few 
days  later  he  went  ofF  hurriedly  to  Antwerp  ;  see  Ep.  934.  8  n. 

John  Louis  Vives  (6  March  1492—6  May  15407  was  a  young  Spaniard  who  was 
just  beginning  to  make  a  reputation.  After  education  in  Valencia,  his  native 
town,  he  came  to  France  c.  1509-10,  probably  to  Paris,  where  for  some  years  he 
studied  in  the  University  ;  also  visiting  Bruges  c.  1512.  His  first  published 
work  is  an  edition  of  Hyginus,  Paris,  J.  Lambert,  s.  a.,  with  a  letter  dated 
31  March  1514,  stating  that  he  was  about  to  lecture  on  it  ;  and  a  short  biographi- 
cal  notice  of  his  teacher,  John  DuUardus  of  Ghent  (fio  Sept.  151 3  ,  printed  in  an 
edition  of  Dullardus'  commentary  on  Aristotle'8  Metheora,  Paris,  T.  Kees,  30  May 
1514.  To  this  period  also  belongshis  Cliristi  Jesu  Trixmphtis,  dedicated  from  Paris, 
April  1514,  to  Bernard  de  Mesa,  who  in  Jan.  1517  became  Bp.  of  Elna  (GC.  vi. 
1066).  Vives  returned  to  the  Netherlands,  probably  to  Bruges  ;  and  in  1516-7 
made  the  acquaintance  of  Erasmus  at  Brussels  {Apol.  qua  respondet,  f°.  A'  ;  Jortiu 
ii.  497).  Later  he  went  to  England  in  search  of  employment  (Ep.  545.  15),  but 
without  success  ;  and  in  1518  he  appears  as  tutor  to  William  Croy  (p.  68)  at 
Louvain,  and  on  termsof  intimacy  with  Erasmus  {Apol.  qua  respondet,  S.  B.  C^  v".  : 
Jortin  ii.  500,  507,.  In  (1519)  Martens  printed  for  him  a  volume  of  Opuscula 
taria,  containing  the  Oiristi  Triumphus  and  many  slight  compositions  addressed 
to  Croy  and  other  pati-ons  (cf.  p.  93).  On  3  March  1520  he  received  licence  to 
teach  privately  in  the  University  (de  Jongh,  p.  20*).  After  Croy's  death  Vives 
remained  at  Louvain,  and,  as  a  part  of  the  collected  editionof  Augustine's  works 
projected  by  Erasmus  (cf.  Ep.  844.  255  n.),  completed  the  De  Ciuitate  Dei,  Basle, 
Froben,  Sept,  1522,  with  a  dedication  to  Henry  vru.  Equipped  with  this  he 
visit«d  England  in  the  autumn,  again  without  the  success  he  wished  ;  thougli 
Henry  acknowledged  the  dedication  with  a  letter,  24  Jan.  1523. 

On  the  deatli  of  Ant.  Nebrissensis  Ep.  487.  i4n.)an  invitation  came  to  Vives 
to  fill  his  chair  at  tlie  University  of  Alcala  ;  sent  through  John  Versara,  6  Sept. 
1522,  from  Valladolid  \Rew.e  Hispanigue  viii,  1901,  pp.  247,  260).  In  May  1523 
therefore  he  determined  to  revisit  Spain  ;  but,  taking  England  on  his  way,  lie 
attracted  the  notice  of  Wolsey,  wlio  sent  him  to  teach  at  Oxford.  He  was 
lodged  in  Foxe's  college  of  Corpus  Christi,  and  was  incorporated  in  the  Univer- 
sity,  10  Oct.  1523.  In  April  1524  he  returned  to  Bruges  and  married,  26  May  ; 
but  in  the  winter  of  1524-5  he  was  again  lecturing  at  Oxford.  Till  1528  he  was 
at  intervals  in  England,  mostly  at  the  Court,  where  he  taught  the  Princess 
Mnry ;  but  for  supporting  the  Queen  about  the  Divorce  he  fell  into  disfavour, 
and  was  even  for  a  time  under  restraint.  Being  driven  from  England  he  settled 
at  Bruges,  and  there  most  of  his  remainingyears  were  spent  ;  one  of  his  visitore, 
in  1529,  being  Ignatius  Loyola.  It  was  his  most  fruitful  literary  period  ;  and 
in  it  he  produced  a  number  of  works  on  educational,  political,  social  and 
religious  questions,  which  have  not  received  from  posterity  their  due  of  recogni- 
tion.  Vives  is  emiuent  among  the  humanists  for  the  importance  that  he  attached 
to  Aristotle  ;  and,  like  Erasmus,  he  frequently  raised  his  voice  on  behalf  of 
international  peace.

FROM   MARTIN   LUTHER  517 


John  Aurifaber,  Jena,  C.  Rhodiua,  1556.  For  convenience  I  have  placed  it  in 
the  same  position  here  as  a  in  Ep.  910. 

Martin  Luther  (10  Nov.  1483?— 18  Feb.  1546),  after  schooling  at  Mansfeld, 
Magdeburg  andEisenach,  had  been  at  Erfurt  University  (B.A.  1502,  M.A.  1505), 
and  then  had  withdrawn,  i-j  July  1505,  into  the  Augustinian  house  at  Erfurt. 
After  receiving  prie.st's  orders  in  1507  he  emerged  in  1508  to  teach  in  the  new 
university  founded  by  Duke  Frederick  of  Saxony  at  Wittenberg.  In  1510-1  he 
made  the  visit  to  Rome  which  so  profoundlj'  impressed  him  ;  and  having  taken 
his  D.D.  19  Oct.  1512,  he  suoceeded  Staupit/  (p.  408)  as  Profeasor  of  Theology  at 
Wittenberg.  For  a  few  years  he  continued  to  live  the  quiet  life  of  a  teachei-, 
and  was  little  known.  He  bad  publislied  nothing,  and  of  the  thousands  of  his 
extant  letters  only  10  are  anterior  to  1516.  But  the  95  theses  directed 
agamst  indulgences  whioh  lie  posted  at  Wittenberg  31  Oct.  1517  (cf.  Ep.  785. 
37  n.)  brought  him  at  once  into  conflict  with  Rome  ;  and  his  writings  soon  began 
to  circulate  in  print  (Ep.  904.  19  n.). 

His  first  comniunication  with  Erasmus  was  in  1516,  when  he  wrote  to  ask, 
througli  Spalatinus,  for  Erasmus'  views  on  a  question  of  theology  (Ep.  501  ;  cf. 
LE*.  25)  ;  but  he  quickly  came  to  perceive  (LE^  34  ;  i  March  1517)  the  funda- 
mental  difference  that  was  to  divide  them.  His  words  there  about  Erasmus, 
'humana  praeualent  in  eo  plus  quam  diuina,'  express  the  position  concisely, 
though  in  a  sense  that  he  hardly  intended  :  the  difference  between  the  humanist 
scholar  seeking  to  advance  knowledge  in  reliance  on  human  reason,  and  the 
religious  leader  contemning  the  things  of  this  world  and  ensuing  human  advance- 
mentand  even  truth  with  aid  from  realms  in  wliich  reasonisnot  always  allowed 
to  have  its  perfect  work. 

Luther  did  his  best  to  minimize  this  diveigence  (LE^.  59,  125  ;  cf.  163.  55). 
When  he  made  the  present  advance  to  Erasmus,  it  was  still  only  latent ;  and  he 
hoped  that  mutual  respect  might  be  possible,  perhaps  even  mutual  help.  A  day 
earlier,  in  dedicating  to  Duke  Frederick  his  commentaries  on  the  Psalms,  he 
had  written  :  '  Ego  pro  mea  temeritate  aleam  ieci,  extrema  semper  tentare  et 
exspectare  pjiratus  '  (LE'^.  166.  81,  2).  Though  he  had  stood  fast  against  Cajetan 
at  Augsburg  in  Oct.  1518,  he  was  still  tremulous,  liis  courage  not  yet  atablished 
by  the  triumph  at  Worms.  His  friends  (cf.  Ep.  938),  even  more  than  himself, 
were  conscious  of  the  dangera  before  him,  and  sought  to  rally  round  him  the 
support  of  men  of  learning. 

Erasmus  on  his  side  knew  Luther  only  by  repute,  though  the  repute  was 
good  (cf.  LE^.  92).  He  had  not  read  Luther's  books  ;  but  he  had  heard  enough 
of  them  to  dissuade  Froben  from  printing  them  (Ep.  904.  19  n.),  and  he  shrank 
instinctively  from  open  strife  as  tending  to  obscure  the  issues.  His  reply, 
therefore,  was  not  cordial,  and  expressed  at  once  his  dislike  of  the  tronbles 
that  Luther's  outspokenness  was  provoking.  Yet  it  was  not  witliout  encourage- 
ment ;  indeed,  as  he  told  Luther,  he  had  already  stood  forward  to  defend  him 
(Ep.  939.  66  seq.),  and  this  defence  he  repeated  to  other  persons  of  influence  (cf. 
Ep.  967.  78  seq.),  though  without  committing  himself  to  Luthers  views. 

As  the  years  went  on,  he  more  and  more  looked  on  Luther  as  retarding  the 
progress  of  a  movement  for  peaceful  reform,  which,  impelled  in  no  small  measure 
Ly  his  own  writings  and  influence,  had  seemed  well  iipon  its  way.  In  the  joy 
of  hattle  and  of  victory  Luther  saw  Erasmus  as  one  who  had  not  been  for  him  ; 
and  a  personal  quarrel  followed,  embittering  their  relations  for  ever.  Luther 
in  his  turn  lived  to  regard  the  advanced  Reformers  as  Erasmus  had  regarded 
him  ;  as  men  who  were  forcing  out  of  his  hands  and  ruining  a  movement  which 
he  considered  his  own.]

Euricius  Cordus  (Henry  Solde)  of  Simtshausen  in  Upper  Hesse  (1486  —  Dec. 
1535)  waa  a  peasanfa  son.  He  was  educated  first  at  Frankenberg  and  then  at 
Marburg  till  autumn  1505;  when  lie  matriculated  at  Erfurt  (B.A.  1507).  After 
marrying  in  1508  he  left  Erfurt,  but  returned  in  1513.  Next  year  he  made 
a  fniitless  attempt  to  find  a  position  iu  Leipzig,  lecturing  on  VergiPs  Bucolics. 
In  1516  he  proceeded  M.A.  at  Erfurt,  and  in  isi^  published  a  volume  of 
Epigraminala,  Erfurt,  M.  Maler  ;  amplified  in  1520  and  1529,  and  containing 
many  addressed  to  or  concerning  Erasmus.  Not  long  aftei-wards  he  was 
appointed  rector  of  the  school  at  8t.  Mary's  in  Erfurt ;  cf.  1.  13.  Failing  of 
prosperity  as  a  teacher,  lie  went  to  Ferrara  to  study  medicine  under  Nix:. 
Leonicenus,  and  met  also  C.  Calcagninus  ''Ep.  611.  24  n.)  and  Manardus.  He 
became  M.D.  1521  and  then  returned  to  Germany. 

By  tliat  time,  like  others  of  his  friends  at  Erfurt  (pp.  407,  413, 602),  he  had  left 
his  early  adniiration  for  Erasmus, aud  wa.s  attached  to  Lutiier ;  w)iom  he  defended 
with  a  pamplilet,  1522.  He  was  town-physician  of  Brunswick  1523-7,  and  then 
went  to  tlie  newly  founded  University  of  Marburg  as  Professor  of  Medicine, 
interesting  liimself  also  in  Eotany  ;  see  his  Botanologicon,  Cologne,  J.  Gymnich, 
1534.  About  Easter  1534  lie  went  to  Bremen  as  town-physician,  but  died  there 
before  long.

I  cannot  definitely  confirm  the  date  ;  but  it  is  not  likely  that  long  elapsed

As  the  letter  is  addressed  to  Basle,  it  can  hardly  be  placed  in  1518,  when 
Erasmus  was  still  at  Louvain  at  this  date.  The  address  may  be  accounted  for 
in  1519  by  supposing  that  Calvus'  last  return  from  Germany  was  in  the  summer 
of  1518  (cf.  Ep.  925.  2  n.),  before  Erasmus  had  left  Basle.]

[By  this  time  Erasmus  was  in  direct  communication  with  Bohemia.  In  the 
Apologia  which  he  prefixed  to  the  new  edition  of  the  New  Testament,  March 
1519»  P-  ^2,  speaking  of  the  wide  recognition  liis  work  was  receiving,  he  says  : 
'Agnoscit  Hungaria,  agnoscit  Bohemia,  episcoporum  ac  summatium  virorum 
literis  mihi  gratias  agens  '.  As  part  of  the  introductory  matter  which  was  still 
unfinished  in  Oct.  1518  (p.  387),  the  Apologia  may  be  dated  about  the  end  of  the 
year.     See  also  Epp.  889.  14,  894.  6. 

.Tohn  Slechta  (+  1522)  of  Wyssehrd,  e.  of  Prague,  after  education  at  Prague 
University  (B.A.  20  Sept.  1483,  M.A.  1484),  was  for  sixteen  years  (1.  5)  a 
secretary  in  the  service  of  Ladislas,  King  of  Bohemia  and  Hungary  (1.  5  n.), 
and  in  that  capacity  wasinstrumental  in  bringing  Balbus  (Ep.  23.  47  n.)  to  teach 
at  Prague  c.  1499— a  step  which,  in  view  of  Balbus'  bad  life,  he  afterwards 
regi-etted.  He  was  strongly  interested  in  humanistic  studies,  and  c.  1500  com- 
poaed  a  dialogue  on  the  relation  of  body  and  soul,  Microcosmus,  which  on  30  April 
1522  he  dedicated  to  Stanislas  Turzo,  Bp.  of  Olmutz  :  but  I  cannot  find  that  it 
was  actually  printed.  About  1507  he  retired  from  the  perturbations  of  the 
Court  and  settled  at  Kosteletz  on  the  Elbe,  ne.  of  Prague,  where  he  occupied 
himself  in  the  education  of  his  son,  and  in  tlie  management  of  his  estates  there 
and  at  Kaurim,  to  the  se.  The  tone  of  his  thouglits  in  later  years  was  grave  and 
serious.  Hisletters  of  that  period  include  a  disquisition  on  the  vices  of  acelibate 
clergy  and  an  exhortation  to  the  duties  of  a  parish  priest  ;  and  it  was  in  the 
same  spirit  that  he  addressed  Erasmus,  perhaps  with  sonie  idea  fcf.  11.  45-7)  of 
vindicating  his  country  from  the  rather  contemptuous  reference  to  it  in  Ep. 
549-  la. 

About  forty  letters  have  been  preserved  of  his  correspondence  ;  some  in  the 
MS.  Lat.  2758  of  the  Prague  Public  Library,  but  mostly  in  the  Lucubratioms  of  his 
intimate  friend,  Bohuslaus  Hassensteyn  (t  13  Nov.  1510),  Prague,  1563  and  1570. 
They  have  been  arranged  and  edited  by  J.  Truhhir  in  the  Sbirka  Pramenuv  ku 
Pozndni  Litercirniho  Zivofa^  Prague,  1893  and  1897  (Boh.  E''  ^).  See  also  Monumenta 
liist.  Vniuers.  Pragen.  ii  -1832  ,  pp.  150-1,  153-4;  where  he  appears  as  John  of 
Blewitz  (near  Schlan,  nw.  of  Prague)  '  Sslechta  cognominatus  '. 

Slechta's  answer  to  thjs  letter,  dated  10  Oct.  from  Kosteletz  (Lond.  xiv.  20. 
LB.  463),  shows  that  Jonas  (Ep.  963.  1  n.)  was  the  bearer  of  this  letter,  and  that 
it  was  not  delivered  till  11  Sept.]

956.    To  Antont  de  la  Marck. 

Parapbrasis  ad  Galatas  f°.  a^  (Louvain.) 

(c.  April  fin.  1519.) 

[The  preface  to  the  Paraphrase  on  Galatians.  This  had  been  begun  in  February 
(Apol.  pro  ded.  matrim.  :  LB.  ix.  112  a),  but  was  interrupted  by  a  series  of 
'  tragedies',  i.  e.  the  necessity  of  replying  to  various  opponents  :  Briard  (p.  93), 
Lee  and  others  (Epp.  946,  952.  17  n.).  A  precise  date  is  not  possible.  The 
passage  in  Ep.  952.  40  seems  to  imply  that  the  Paraphrase  was  not  yet  completed. 
If  that  inference  be  accepted,  tlie  preface  may  be  dated  about  the  end  of  April. 

The  first  edition  is  by  Martens,  Louvain,  May  1519  ("a  ,  reprinted  by  Froben 
in  August  (j3).  It  was  printed  again  by  Froben  with  Romans  (Ep.  710)  and 
Corinthians  (Ep.  916)  in  Jan.  1520  without  change  ;  but  there  are  marks  of  revi- 
sion  in  Froben's  collected  editions  of  March  1521  (7)  and  July  (8).  The  preface 
appears  without  further  change  in  Froben's  editions  of  Feb.  and  May  1522  ;  but 
after  that  it  was  removed — for  an  obvious  reason — ,  and  in  the  later  collections 
this  Paraphrase  was  printed  without  any  dedication.  A  copy  of  a  was  sent  to 
England  on  25  May  1519  (cf.  Ep.  974  .  On  32  Aug.  1519  Boniface  Amerbaeh 
writes  to  Zasius  that  0  is  not  yet  finished  (Basle  MS.  D.  IV.  i8.  157). 

Antony  (c.  1495-1523),  son  of  Robert  de  la  Marck  (p.  182},  at  an  early  age 
began  to  acquire  preferment.  In  Jan.  1515  he  was  Canon  of  Liege.  On  18  March 
1516  he  surrendered  to  Aleander  {Jmrnal,  ed.  Omont,  pp.  17,  31)  his  claim  ou 
the  Provostship  of  St.  John's  at  Liege  ;  and  in  the  spring  of  1517  he  was  Arch- 
deacon  of  Brabant  (AI.  E.  ii,  p.  357).  In  1518  he  received  the  Cluniac  Abbey  of 
Beaulieu  in  Argonne,  sw.  of  Verdun,  of  which  his  uncle,  the  Bp.  of  Liege  (p.  167), 
was  perpetual  administrator  ;  and  in  1520  he  was  Archdeacon  of  Chartres.  He 
seems  to  have  attempted  to  secure  some  preferment  for  Erasmus,  but  with- 
out  success  (Lond.  xv.  11,  LB.  386;.  As  Abbot,  tbe  rapacity  of  his  oflScials  and 
his  own  licentious  conduct  soon  made  him  odious  to  his  neighbours.  For  pro- 
tection  he  meditated  reverting,  like  his  uncle,  to  the  Burgundian  allegiance. 
But  before  he  could  effect  this,  his  abbey  was  stormed  by  the  French,  and  he 
himself  was  stabbed  to  death  by  a  neighbouring  landowner,  whose  daughter  he 
had  wronged. 

See  P.  A.  Lemaire,  Recherches  sur  Beaulieu  en  Argonne,  1873,  pp.  71-4,  148  ;  and 
C4C.  xiii.  1268,9.]

[The  import  of  the  series  of  letters  addressed  to  England  at  this  time 
(Epp.  961-2,  964-7)  is  quite  clear.  Without  making  a  direct  request,  Erasmus 
intimated  that  he  woukl  be  glad  to  return  and  settle  there,  if  suitable  proTision 
could  be  made  for  him— provision,  of  course,  vphich  should  ensure  him  leisure 
and  not  infringe  his  independence. 

When  he  last  left  Englnnd  he  had  felt  himself  secure,  without  need  to  look  to 
English  help  (Ep.  577).  He  had  taken  service  with  Charles  CEp.  370.  18  n.),  and 
his  allegiance  required  tliat  he  should  settle  in  the  Netherlands  :  the  revision  of 
the  New  Testament  was  occupying  his  thoughts,  and  the  way  seemed  open  for 
him  to  complete  and  print  it.  But  in  two  years  his  world  had  changed.  The 
New  Testament  was  indeed  finished  ;  but  it  had  brought  many  enemies,  and 
Louvain  had  become  a  less  pleasant  home  than  he  had  expected.  Charles  had 
gone  oflf  to  Spain  (Epp.  948.  195,  969.  16, 970. 13;,  the  promised  pension  only  once 
paid  (Ep.  597.  26n.).  Le  Sauvage,  whom  he  regarded  as  his  special  patron 
(Ep.  887.  8,9  ;  cf.  Ep.  436 j,  was  dead  ;  and  the  oflFer  from  Ferdinand  (p.  492)  did 
not  attract  him.  Under  these  circumstances  it  is  not  surprising  that  he  should 
have  bethought  himself  to  accept  (cf.  Epp.  825.  14-5,  855.  28-9)  one  of  the 
numerous  invitations  he  had  received  in  recent  years  (Ep.  809.  127-33). 

From  England  in  particular  these  had  been  promising  (Ep.  694.  10),  though 
somewhat  elusive  when  he  showed  signs  of  wishing  to  accept  them  (Epp.  775. 
18-21,  784.  54-7,  786.  34-40,  806.  13-4).    Henry  had  assured  him  he  should  have

him  on  the  same  footing  as  liis  junior,  Clement,  and  his  pupil,  Lupset.  Or  on  his

the  resources  of  the  printers  were  small  (cf.  Ep.  283.  162  n.).  But  whatever  the 
reason,  England  saw  him  no  more.]

[Sir  Henry  Guildford  {1489 —  May  1532)  was  a  personal  friend  of  Henry  vili, 
than  whom  he  was  a  year  or  two  older.  From  his  youth,  through  the  position 
of  his  parents  (1.  46  n.),  he  was  closely  connected  with  the  Court,  taking  part 
firat  in  the  revels  and  then  in  matters  of  confidence.  He  won  fame  at  the  wars, 
being  knighted  by  Ferdinand  of  Spain  in  Sept.  151 1  at  the  close  of  an  expedition 
against  the  Moors,  and  becoming  Henry'3  standard-bearer  in  May  1513  during 
the  invasion  of  France.  The  King's  reliance  upon  him  increased  continnally, 
and  he  filled  one  post  of  trast  after  another;  finally  being  appointed  Controller 
of  the  Royal  household.     See  DNB.    His  portrait  by  Holbein  is  at  Windsor. 

The  present  letter,  which  ia  clearly  contemporary  with  Epi>.  961,  964,  ^6^, 
is  an  indication  of  the  influenoe  with  the  King  that  he  was  considered  to 
enjoy.]

990.      TO   JOHN    CLAyMOND. 

Farrago  p.  64.  Louvain. 

F.  p.  231 :  HN:  Lond.  iv.  n  :  LB.  438.  27  June  1519. 

[Between  the  foundation  of  Corpus  and  the  publication  of  the  Farrago  (E)  1519 
is  the  only  year  in  'which  Erasmus  was  at  Louvain  at  this  time. 

John  Claymond  or  Claimond  (c.  1457  —  19  Nov.  1537J  of  Frampton  in  Lincoln- 
shire,  spent  most  of  his  life  in  Oxford.  He  was  a  Demy  of  Magdalen  in  1483, 
Fellow  1488,  and  President  1504  :  B.D.  1508,  D.D.  1510.  About  1487  he  became 
known  to  Foxe,  who  gave  him  the  Mastership  of  St.  Cross  Hospital  near  Win- 
chester  1505-24,  and  in  151 7  persuaded  him  to  leave  Magdalen  and  preside  over 
the  new  foundatiou,  Corpus  Chriati.  This  oflBce  he  held  until  his  deatb  ;  and 
during  his  life  lie  also  held  benefices  in  the  counties  of  Somerset,  Hants,  Durham, 
and  Worcester.  He  was  a  man  of  exceptional  public  spirit  and  of  great  sincerity 
of  character.  Erasmus,  who  had  perhaps  met  him  in  Oxlord  in  1499,  speaks  of 
him  always  as  a  theologian  ;  but  his  only  known  work  is  some  collections  for 
notes  on  Pliny  N.  H.,  ■which  exist  in  ms.  in  the  CoUege  library  and  also  in 
duplicate  in  the  Library  at  Basle  :  the  former  mostly  autograph,  the  latter 
partially  so.  He  is  also  credited  with  notes  on  Plautiis  and  Grellius.  Vives 
found  him  a  friend  and  patron  (Vi.  E.  S.  14  v°,  25,  44).  In  Feb.  1526  Erasmus 
dedicated  to  him  translations  of  Chrysostom's  De  fato  and  Da  prouide-ntia  Dei.  In 
the  summer  of  1531  Simon  Grynaeus  received  assistance  from  him  on  a  visit  to 
Oxford  in  search  of  MSS.  to  be  printed  at  Basle  :  see  the  preface  to  Plato  and 
Proclus,  Basle,  J.  Valder,  March  1534,  and  CIaymond's  letter  of  13  May  (1532) 
in  Grynaeus'  Epistolae,  Basle,  J.  Oporinus,  Oct.  1556,  f.  161.  Among  the  Corpus 
MSS.  (318.  23,  ed.  H.  0.  Coxe)  is  an  autograph  letter  written  by  Linacre  from 
London  to  Claymond  when  President  of  Magdalen,  sending  him  a  pupil  and 
urging  him  to  leam  Greek.

[The  dates  are  corroborated  by  the  movemeiits  of  Erasmus  and  Andronicus. 

Tranquillus  Parthenius  Andronicus  was  a  native  of  Ragusa  in  Dalmatia,  his 
second  name  being  derived  from  the  Partheni,  who  in  ancient  times  inhabited 
that  region.  This  witty  and  versatile  adventurer,  after  a  round  of  Italian 
Universities  —  Padua,  Bologna,  Siena,  Perugia,  Eome  —  appears  (c.  1517  at 
Vienna)  soliciting  the  aid  of  Vadianus  and  offering  to  lecture  on  Quintilian  and 

50.  sint  E  :  sunt  H.  53.  ille  N.         54.  ipsl  add.  H.         61.  lul.  F :  lulii  H. 


622  LETTERS   OF  EKASMUS  [151 9 

Cicero  (VE.  s'.  29).  Perhaps  c.  Sept.  1517  he  contributed  some  verses  (f.  38)  to 
Eck's  edition  of  Dionysius  the  Areopagite's  De  mystica  tkeologia,  Augsburg,  J.  Miller, 
25  May  1519  (see  Wiedemann^s  Eck,  pp.  495-9 "i;  and  in  Oct.  others  (f°.  a')  to 
Vadianus'  edition  of  Pomponius  Mela,  Vienna,  J.  Singren,  May  1518.  Vadianus 
passed  him  on  to  Urban  Regius  at  Ingolstadt  in  Nov.  (VE.  107) ;  and  he  wasstill 
there  in  March  1518,  when  he  produced  a  poem  against  the  Turks  (Biicking, 
Hutteni  Opp.  v.  205-16).  In  May  he  was  at  Augsburg,  where  Miller  printed 
an  oration  by  him  on  the  same  theme,  addressed  to  Maximilian  (ibid.  217-228). 
Later  he  matriculated  at  Leipzig,  and  having  made  a  name  with  an  oration 
De  laudibus  eloquentiae,  23  Aug.  (printed  by  Lotther  c.  25  Aug.  ;  Proctor  ii.  1 1368), 
in  which  he  describes  himself  (f.  A^)  as  of  '  immatura  aetas  ',  he  was  appointed 
to  lecture  through  the  wintfr  on  Quintilian  :  but  for  his  reputation  there  see 
Ep.  911.  44-6.  A  letter  from  him  to  Pirckheimer,  3  Jan.  1519,  thanks  for 
hospitality  sliown  at  Nuremberg  Tleumann  li).  In  the  spring  he  left  Leipzig 
and  came  to  visit  Erasmus  at  Louvain  ;  perhaps  by  way  of  Erfurt,  if  some  verses 
addresscd  to  him  in  Eobanus'  Syluae,  bk.  iii,  belong  to  this  period.  Missing 
Erasmus  he  went  on,  perhaps  to  Paris  (cf.  1.  88  n.). 

After  this  his  life  can  only  be  traced  at  intervals.  He  perhaps  came  again  into 
Erasmus'  circle  :  for  there  is  a  character  named  Parthenius  in  the  Conuiuium 
Poeticum,  first  printed  in  Froben's  edition  of  the  CoUoquies,  Aug.  1523. 

In  1527  he  published  a  dialogue,  Sylia,  s.  L,  in  defence  of  Diocletian,  addressed  to 
John  Lascaris.  In  June  1530  he  was  ambassador  of  John  Zapolya,  the  claimant 
King  of  Hungary,  employed  at  Constantinople  (T.  Wierzbowski,  Materyaly  do 
Dziej(hD  Piimiennictica  Polskiego,  i,  1900,  p.  39)  ;  and  in  Oct.  1531  he  was  still  there 
(Brewer  v.  471).  By  1543  he  was  secretary  to  Ferdinand,  and  June-Aug.  was 
sent  by  him  to  England  to  ask  for  aid  against  the  Turks  (ibid.  xviii.  i.  659,  894, 
925,  ii.  26)  ;  and  in  May  1545  he  was  in  Cracow,  perhaps  on  a  similar  mission, 
when  he  composed  an  Admxmilio  to  the  nobles  of  Poland,  Cracow,  H.  Vietor,  1545, 
exhorting  them  to  avoid  the  internal  schisms  whioh  had  caused  the  downfall  of 
Hungary.]

APPENDIX  XII 

THE   EPISTOLAE    SELECTAE   PER   BARLANDVM,  1520 

In  December  1520  Martens  published  at  Louvain  a  volume  entitled 
Epistolae  aliquot  selectae  ex  Erasmicis  prr  Hadnanum  Barlatuhtm.  In 
the  preface  Barland  states  that  Martens  had  requested  him  to  select 
some  of  the  shorter  letters  '  ex  magno  epistolarum  Erasmi  volumine ', 
for  publication  as  a  schoolbook.  The  '  magnum  volumen  '  is,  of 
course,  the  Farrago  (E),  which  had  appeared  in  OctoV>er  i,"i9-  Of 
the  123  letters  -which  the  selection  contains,  115  are  derived  from 
E,  6  are  not  in  E  but  appear  in  the  Epistolae  ad  diuersos  (F),  Aug. 
1521,  and  2  are  not  found  elsewhere  than  in  this  volume  of  selec- 
tions.  We  are  indebted,  as  so  often  before,  to  the  kindness  of  the  late 
M.  Vander  Haeghen  of  Ghent ;  who  by  lending  us  a  copy  of  Barland's 
volume  has  rendered  possible  a  minute  examination  of  its  contents. 
And  a  careful  collation  by  niy  wife  of  the  variants  between  E  and  F 
has  indicated  clearly  the  position  occupied  by  this  book  relatively  to 
those  two  editions. 

The  date  of  the  preparation  of  F  has  been  involved  in  some 
obscurity,  and  it  has  been  possible  to  infer  that  the  printing  of  the 
book  was  far  advanced  at  a  time  when  in  fact  Erasmus  had  not  yet 
begun  the  uecessary  work  of  revision.  This  obscurity  has  arisen 
from  a  wrong  year-date,  1.520,  added  in  the  Opus  Epistolarum  (H), 
1529,  to  Erasmus'  preface  to  F,  addressed  to  Beatus  Rhenanus  from 
Louvain,  27  May.  In  this  preface,  Lond.  i.  i.  LB.  ,'07,  Erasmus 
says  that  he  had  revised  the  letters  ah-eady  published,  and  sent  them 
to  be  printed  by  Froben  ;  who  at  the  time  of  wiiting  '  iam  .  .  ad  xli. 
senionem  peruenit'.  E  and  its  predecessors,  C^,  B.  D*,  as  reprinted 
in  F,  reach  p.  472,^  including  a  few  new  letters,  amongst  them 
Epp.  361,  392,  540,  605,  inserted  out  of  place  in  order  to  be  next 
the  letters  they  answer  ;  and  the  fortieth  sheet  ends  on  p.  478.* 
We  may  take  it,  therefore,  that  Froben's  words,  which  Erasmus 
repeats,  meant  that  he  had  completed  the  reprinting  of  E  and  its 
predecessors,  and  was  ready  to  begin  on  the  forty-first  sheet. 

Now  on  p.  478  of  F  a  letter  is  printed  (Lond.  xii.  rr,  LB.  535) 
which  bears  date  4  Oct.  1520  ;  and  on  p.  534  another  (Lond.  xiv.  3, 
LB,  591)  with  the  date  24  Aug.  i?,2i.  Counting  the  time  occupied 
in  the  transit  of  Froben's  letter  to  Louvain,  and  of  copies  of  Erasmus' 
letters  to  Basle — perhaps  a  foi-tnight  each  way — we  may  reckon  that 
if  Erasmus'  preface  to  F  is  reaUy  to  be  dated  in  ^520,  Froben  must 
have  waited  about  five  raonths,  May — Oct.  r,=;20,  before  advancing 
six  pages,  472-8  ;  and  nearly  sixteen  months,  May  ^520  —  Sept.  152^, 
before   pi-inting   62  pages;   a  rate  of  progress  which   is  not  only 

1  The  page-numbers  214,  215  are  duplicated  in  F  through  an  ovorsight.

most  improbable  in  itself,  but  also  quite  at  variance  with  his  rapidity 
in  printing  the  New  Testament  (Ep.  384  introd.).  It  may  fairly  be 
concluded,  therefore,  that  Erasmus'  preface  to  F  is  to  be  dated  1521  ; 
a  conclusion  which  is  supported  by  the  fact  that  it  is  printed  on  the 
first  and  final  sheet,  a,  with  only  two  other  letters,  which  are  dated 
13  Aug.  and  14  Oct.  1521. 

External  evidence  also  is  available  to  corroborate  this  result.  In 
July  1520  Erasmus  writes  to  Mosellanus  that  lie  is  preparing  a  revi- 
sion  of  the  Farrago  ;  ^  and  on  30  Nov.  he  tells  Barland  that  the  work 
is  done.-  Further,  in  a  letter  of  (c.  Jan.)  152 1,  Froben'  announces 
to  Boniface  Amerbach  at  Avignon  that  Erasmus  has  sent  '  Epistolare 
suum  \  Under  these  circumstances  it  is  evident  that  Barland's 
volume  is  prior  to  F  in  time. 

That  Barland's  collection  was  taken  in  the  main  from  E  is  shown 
by  the  various  readings.  Of  the  115  letters  which  it  reprints 
from  E,  just  half  (58)  have  no  variants  in  F  ;  but  of  the  remain- 
ing  .57,  41  invariably  follow  E  where  it  differs  from  F.  Two 
letters,  Epp.  279  and  821,  appear  in  both  D  and  E,  and  are  in 
consequence  twice  reprinted  in  F.  In  each  case  Barland'3  text 
follows  EF-  nine  times,  as  against  DF'  once  :  the  single  exceptions 
being,  in  Ep.  279.  13  nauim  (f'.  d^)  for  nauem,  in  Ep.  821.  6  iuuat 
(f".  b^)  for  imief,  both  perhaps  merely  accidental. 

There  are,  however,  two  more  categories,  4  letters  in  which 
Barland's  text  follows  sometimes  E  and  sometimes  F,  and  ro 
letters  in  which  it  follows  F  against  E.  In  Ep.  56  (f".  k  v<^.)  Bar- 
land  follows  E  in  11.  16,  26,  and  F  in  11.  14,23,  35.  In  Ep.  123  (f".  k) 
Barland  follows  E  in  11.  19,  23,  and  F  in  11.  6,  8,  15,  18,  26.  In  Ep.

As  to  the  final  category,  in  Ep.  54  (f".  i^  vo.)  Barland  has  the

(f '.  i*)  the  easy  corrections  made  in  F :  in  Ep.  1 48  (f'^.  i'')  the  readings

Ep.  225  (f".  k^  V".)  the  correction  in  1.  20:  in  Ep.  252  (f'.  k^)  the

(f'^.  k''  Y'.)  the  variation  in  the  opening  word. 

From  the  decided  character  of  some  of  the  changes  in  this  last

and  this  fact  coupled  with  the  inclusion  in  Barland's  volume  of  six 
new  letters  which  were  subsequently  printed  in  F,  indicates  that 
Erasmus  must  have  sanctioned  the  undertaking.  It  may  also  be 
inferred  that  he  did  not  begin  to  interest  himself  in  the  book  until 
it  was  nearing  completion.  The  new  letters  are  all  at  the  end,  Nos.

From  these  details  the  story  of  Barland's  Ej^istoJar  sclectar  may  be

ing  a  few  of  the  new  letters  which  he  had  selected  for  publication.

had  Erasmus'  concurrence,  it  is  evident  that  for  such  new  matter  as 
it  contains,  it  is  the  archetype.

The  Royal  Library  at  Copenhagen  possesses  a  MS.  (G.  K.  S.  95  fol.) 
of  253  folios,  which  is  almost  entirely  in  the  handwriting  of  Erasmus.

manuscript.  It  Avas  presented  to  the  library  })y  Frederick  III  of 
Denmark  (1648-1670);  and  its  binding  is  probaVdy  of  that  period. 
Its  contents  also  are  so  varied  that  they  do  not  give  any  clear 
indication  as  to  the  mode  of  its  composition. 

They  are  as  follows  : —

Greek,  in  the  hand  of  a  secretary.

what  hastily  Avritten  ;  the  leaves  not  always  correctly  arranged, 
as  the  following  scheme  will  show  : —

With  the  exception  of  the  letters,  which  are  somewhat  diverse  in 
date,  the  manuscript  Ijelongs  to  only  a  few  years  of  Erasmus'  life. 
As  to  when  he  l>egan  to  write  the  Ecciesiastes,  there  is  no  definite 
evidence  to  show.    It  had  been  asked  for  by  his  friends  as  far  back  as

151 9  (Ep.  932.  16-S),  and  by  Jan.  1523  Iie  had  made  some  notes  which 
he  hoped  to  work  up  Ijefore  the  close  of  the  year  (i.  p.  34.  19-22  and 
crit.  n.).  After  the  puhlication  of  Cat.  Liic.  (i)  the  fulfihnent  of  the 
promise  was  often  claimed.  But  from  the  tribute  paid  to  the  memor}- 
of  Warham  (t  22  Aug.  1532)  it  is  clear  that  this  draft  at  any  rate — 
and  there  is  no  evidence  to  show  that  there  was  any  other— cannot 
have  been  begun  before  1532-3  ;  for  the  passage  occurs  (f.  35)  in 
continuous  composition  and  cannot  l>e  considered  as  an  insei-tion. 
It  was  not  till  the  spring  of  1535  that  Erasmus  I>egan  to  print  ;  but 
as  there  are  five  books,  and  as  he  suffei'ed  much  from  illness  during 
his  closing  years.  Book  I,  with  which  we  are  now  concerned.  may 
well  have  been  begun  at  the  time  suggested.  This  conclusiun  is 
bome  out  by  the  paper  used.  In  the  Ecclesiastrs  there  is  only  one 
watermark,  and  it  occurs  30  times.  The  same  occurs  on  30  out  of 
38  sheets  in  the  Adagia  ;  on  2  out  of  8  sheets  in  the  De  praepurutione  ; 
and  in  all  the  letters  written  in  1533. 

The  De  praeparutione  ud  moriem  was  written  in  response  to  a  letter 
(EE'.  109)  from  Thomas  Boleyn,  Earl  of  Wiltshire,  dated  19  June 
(1533)-  The  preface,  which  in  the  manuscript  has  no  date,  in  the 
printed  book  (L)  js  dated  i  Dec.  1533. 

The  additions  to  the  enlarged  edition  of  the  Adugiu,  Basle,  Frol»en, 
and  Episcopius,  March  1533,  number  3659-4146;  and  of  these  the 
manuscript  contains  rather  more  than  half.  The  preface  which  pre- 
cedes  them  on  p.  989  of  the  printed  volume.  is  dated  i  Oct.  1532  ; 
and  in  Q.  7,  dated  15  Jan.  (1533  ,  Erasmus  discusses  the  interpreta- 
tion  to  be  put  on  a  phrase  which  was  afterwards  included  as  No.  4082. 
They  were  probably,  therefore,  composed  for  the  most  part  in  1532-3. 
No.  1493  ^^  ^-^^  manuscript  is  a  new  version  of  the  adage,  which 
appears  for  the  first  time  in  the  edition  of  1536. 

The  notes  on  Seneca  were  made  for  the  Froben  edition  of  March 
1529;  those  on  Augustine  I  have  not  been  able  to  trace.  The 
Froben  firm  published  Augustine's  works  in  1528-9  and  1540-3 
with  the  aid  of  Erasmus  ;  but  I  cannot  find  these  notes  in  either 
edition.

The  arrangement  of  the  volume  as  it  is  now  bound,  shows  little 
evidence  of  design.  The  letters  are,  indeed,  placed  together  at  the 
end  ;  but  the  other  compositions  are  in  a  confusion  from  which 
a  very  slight  expenditure  of  trouble  would  have  extricated  them  ; 
and  it  may  therefore  be  safely  assumed  that  the  manuscript  collection 

in  whatever  manner  it  was  formed — was  sent  to  the  binder  in  the 

condition  in  which  it  happened  to  be.     We  may  argue.  therefore,  that 
the  collection  was  not  made  by  any  one  interested  in  the  papers  for

their  historical  value  ;  for  in  that  case  we  might  fairly  expect  to  find 
them  carefully  sorted  out  and  the  letters  especially  placed  in  chrono- 
logical  order.  It  seems  more  as  though  it  were  a  congeries  brought 
together  almost  haphazard  Ijy  some  one  desirous  of  gathering  and  yet 
hardly  heeding  what  he  gathered  :  as  for  instance  Lambert  Comannus, 
Erasmus'  last  secretary,  might  have  laid  his  hands  hastily  on  such 
papers  as  he  could  find  after  his  masters  death.  For  this  suggestion 
there  is  some  confirmation  in  the  fact  that,  notwithstanding  what 
has  l^een  said,  there  is  a  certain  degree  of  arrangement  about  the 
papers.  In  the  Ecclesiastes  and  other  compositions  the  displacement 
which  occurs  is  not  of  single  sheets  )>ut,  as  has  )jeen  shown  al>ove, 
of  groups  ;  and  again  among  the  letters  there  is  some  natural  group- 
ing.  Thus  the  three  letters  which  are  printed  in  the  De  Prae- 
2)arafione,  1534  (L),  occur  together  at  the  beginning  ;  and  of  the  18 
which  appear  in  the  EjAstolue  Floridae,  1531  (J),  17  are  found  in  a 
continuous  series,  which  at  times  foUows  very  dosely  the  order  in 
which  they  are  printed  in  the  book.  This  orderly  and  yet  disordered 
arrangement  is  just  what  might  be  expected  in  a  collection  hurriedly 
gathered  during  the  necessaiy  dispositions  which  foUow  death  ;  and 
it  is  not  difficult  to  suppose  that  the  papers  may  sulisequently  have 
passed  from  hand  to  hand  without  much  serutiny  until  they  reached 
the  protection  of  the  Copenhagen  Library. 

The  collection  has  considerable  value  in  the  light  that  it  throws 
on  Erasmus'  practice  in  the  writing  and  preservation  of  his  corre- 
.spondence.  All  the  letters  are  rough  drafts,  not  a  single  one  having 
been  actually  dispatched,  and  a  few  being  back  to  back  on  the  same 
sheet.  There  is  thus  proof  of  a  fact  for  which  there  is  no  other 
direct  evidence,  that  Erasmus  in  his  later  years  usually  wrote  rougli 
drafts  of  his  letters,  and  that  these  were  copied  fair  by  his  secretaries 
for  dispatch.  A  numVier  of  fair  copies  written  by  secretaries  are  of 
course  in  existence  ;  but  except  for  those  under  consideration  here  no 
rough  drafts  are  known.  This  later  practice  is  in  direct  contrast  to 
that  of  the  period  1516-8,  which  is  represented  by  the  Deventer 
Letter-book  (App.  8),  when  he  commonly  wrote  his  letters  for  dispatch 
and  his  secretaries  copied  them  for  preservation. 

The  letters  bear  various  marks  of  revision,  besides  the  corrections 
naturally  made  at  the  time  of  first  writing.  Two  of  the  letters  of 
1524  have  been  corrected.  One,  f.  243,  was  unquestionably  revised 
by  Erasmus,  V>ut  as  in  one  place  there  are  two  divergences  from  the 
Opus  Epistolarinn,  1529  (H),  the  edition  in  which  it  was  first  printed, 
it  seems  doubtful  whether  the  corrections  were  made  with  a  view  to 
its  publication  there.  More  probaVjly  they  were  made  a  few  years 
earlier,  and  su))sequently  improved  at  the  time  of  printing.  The 
other  letter  of  1524,  f.  239,  presents  difficulties.  There  are  six  cor- 
rections  by  a  contemporary  hand,  which  might  Ije  Ei-asmus',  but 
might  equaUy  well  )>e  that  of  his  secretary.  Here  again  the  cor- 
rections  cannot  have  )jeen  made  with  a  view  to  H,  for  of  the  numerous 
changes  made  there  none  that  are  really  important  are  found  iu 
these  six.  So  that  here  too  we  may  attri)jute  them  to  a  revision 
at  an  earlier  time. 

Three  letters  of  1528  show  revision,  of  a  different  kind  in  each 
case.     In  one,  f.  198,  Erasmus  is  clearly  the  author  of  the  changes,

which  consist  of  slight  polishings  of  pbrase  and  also  of  substitutions 
of  periphrases  for  proper  names,  publication  of  which  would  be  likely 
to  cause  offence.  But  it  is  noticeable  that  two  of  the  corrections 
made  have  ):)een  further  altered  before  printing  in  H.  In  another, 
f.  196,  a  secretary  has  copied  into  the  text  a  word  written  by  Erasmus 
in  the  margin.  But  in  the  third,  f.  1 80,  the  treatment  is  more  thorough. 
There  are  a  few  coiTections,  mostly  marginal,  ]>y  Erasmus,  which 
are  probably  of  the  time  of  first  writing.  But  another  hand,  working 
with  a  finer  pen,  has  improved  the  writing  throughout  the  page  to 
make  it  more  legible  ;  not  introducing  any  changes,  however,  except 
in  the  alteration  of  -e  to  -ae  by  addition  of  the  cedilla.  It  is  hardly 
possible  from  its  character  that  this  should  be  the  work  of  Erasmus. 
It  is  proljably,  however,  contemporary,  and  may  therefore  be  attributed 
to  a  secretary  preparing  the  document  for  copying. 

The  most  interesting  case  of  revision  is  in  ff.  207-220,  Avhich  con- 
tain  the  letters  of  the  years  1 530-1.  These  have  been  clearly  and 
definitely  revised  by  Erasmus,  with  a  finer  pen  aud  darker  ink  which 
is  easUy  distinguishable.  Beyond  f.  220,  though  the  letters  are  still 
of  the  same  period  and  are  printed  in  the  same  volunie,  J,  the  revision 
ceases.  Of  one  of  these  letters,  f.  217,  the  letter  actually  sent  still 
survives ;  and  by  comparison  of  the  texts  it  is  clear  that  Erasmus' 
corrections  were  not  made  for  reproduction  in  the  letter  sent.  There 
can  therefore  be  no  doubt  that  the  corrections  in  the  whole  series 
were  made  somewhat  later,  with  a  view  to  the  publication  of  the 
letters  in  J.  It  is  to  be  noticed,  however,  that,  as  with  H,  the  cor- 
rections  made  by  Erasmus  on  these  leaves  are  by  no  means  all  those 
that  appear  in  J.  Besides  Erasmus'  revision  there  are  also  two 
cases,  ff.  209-1  c,  where  improvement  of  the  writing  like  that  noticed 
on  f.  180  has  taken  place. 

Except  in  one  case  there  is  no  sign  that  any  part  of  the  manuscript 
was  ever  used  for  printing.  The  exception  is  the  first  letter  in  the 
collection  (f.  160),  which  is  the  final  one  in  the  De  purifafe  (M).  It 
is  not,  however,  really  a  letter,  but  is  of  the  nature  of  a  preface  ;  so 
that  no  fair  copy  of  it  would  be  needed  for  dispatch.  It  is  moreover 
well  and  clearly  written  ;  and  so  it  is  not  surprising  that  it  should 
exhibit  the  familiar  red  chalk  marks  with  which  printers  used  to 
record  on  copy  the  divisionsand  numbers  of  pages — in  this  casethose 
of  M.  But  the  chalk  marks  occur  nowhere  else,  either  among  the 
compositions  or  the  letters  ;  and  the  manuscript  as  a  whole  is  clean 
and  free  from  folds  or  marks  of  use.  It  is  clear  therefore  that  it  was 
not  used  for  the  press.  The  improvement  noted  above  in  various 
letters  may  accordingly  be  attributed  to  a  preparation  of  the  text 
for  copying  with  a  view  to  use  in  the  press ;  and  was  perhaps  done 
by  one  secretary  for  the  guidance  of  anotber. 

The  work  of  secretaries  is  also  shown  in  the  names  of  persons 
addressed  which  are  prefixed  by  them  to  some  of  the  letters  ;  by  the 
entries  '  Transcripta '  (ff.  181  and  232)  and  '  Transcriptae  sunt  omnes ' 
(f.  201)  ;  and  by  vertical  lines  drawn  down  the  page  in  some  cases, 
clearly  conveying  the  same  signification.  In  a  few  places  too  they 
have  underlined  words  wbich  they  found  diflBcult  to  read  ;  and  on 
one  page  (f.  218)  an  underUning  pen  seems  to  have  drawn  Erasmus' 
attention  to  two  cases  of  repetition,  which  he  subsequently  corrected.

Indeed  miswritings  in  the  letters  are  not  uncomnion,  many  of  them 
being  very  rapidly  written :  so  that  it  is  not  surprising  to  find  the 
printed  version  sometimes  at  fault. 

In  the  two  ca.ses  (ff.  184.  21-)  whei-e  we  have  the  opportunity  of 
comparing  the  rough  drafts  ^vith  the  fair  copies  actually  sent,  it  is 
noticeable  that  the  secretary  was  not  scrupulously  accurate  in  his 
copying,  as  we  have  seen  ah-eady  with  Ep.  326  ;  writing  for  instance 
cuni  for  titm,  qnum  for  cum,  besides  -ae  for  -e  and  making  occa-^ional 
differences  of  punctuation  and  order. 

The  manuscript  volume  presents  us  with  ample  material  for  an 
examination  of  Erasmus'  orthography.  It  appears  that  he  uses  the 
form  -e  far  more  commonly  than  -ae  ;  which  rarely  occurs  except 
as  -§.  In  a  few  cases  (ff.  213,  214.  219  V.)  in  revising  Erasmus  adds 
a  cedilla  to  an  -e  ;  but  this  is  quite  exceptional.  The  form  acditio, 
which  with  its  kindred  words  is  regularlj'  printed  by  the  Froben 
press,  has  hardly  any  authority  in  this  manuscript,  editio  being 
Erasmus'  ahnost  invariable  usage  :  though  aed-  occurs  thrice,  on 
ff.  160-1,  and  an  improving  hand,  not  Erasmus',  has  added  a  cedilla 
once,  on  f,  209,  Again  litterae — one  of  the  words  about  which  it  i& 
difBcult  to  coUect  evidence,  because  in  manuscript  it  is  so  frequently 
contracted — is  almost  always  found  instead  of  Uterae.  Ptj  occurs 
only  rarely,  as  also  pre,  the  contracted  form  being  usually  adopted. 
Sometimes  it  is  quite  impossible  to  determine  certainly  what 
Erasmus  wrote.  The  vowels  are  often  so  alike  that  the  only  guide 
is  in  the  sense,  and  where  this  fails  there  is  no  arbiter.  The  same 
word,  for  example,  might  not  infrequently  be  read  either  possum, 
possini  or  possem  ;  nolim  or  )wlui ;  and  the  terminations  -is  and  -ius 
are  often  indistinguishable.
